poiFRA-desc:
Franco-Iberia stands as a testament to the resilience and adaptability of {{poiFRA005|human civilization}} in the face of catastrophe. Born from the fractured remnants of the Old European Union, it is more than just a nation—it is a symbol of unity forged through adversity.

While Europe avoided the most immediate devastation of the Great Mistake, it was soon overwhelmed by the ripple effects of global upheaval. Massive waves of refugees fleeing the chaos in Asia reshaped the continent, straining resources and exposing deep divides within the Old Union. Disagreements over priorities—whether to address the humanitarian crisis or prepare for environmental threats—splintered the fragile alliance. In the end, these pressures proved insurmountable, and the Old Union collapsed under the weight of its internal conflicts.

It can be said, and it is said, that Franco-Iberia is the spiritual child of the former European Union. While {{poiFRA001|its territorial claims}} seem to indicate that its goal is to {{poiFRA003|dominate the continent}} once and for all, {{poiFRA004|some of its leaders}} are still squabbling over how to approach it.

One of the country's most important components is {{poiFRA006|the Mediterranean Sea}}, which is essential for the Union's exports, with important trading partners in {{poiFRA012|the Mediterranean Bloc}} such as {{poiFRA009|Padania}}, {{poiFRA011|Greece}} and even the Maghreb. Still, {{poiFRA002|important emerging powers}} want to unseat Franco-Iberia from its position of economic hegemony, clashing head-on with {{poiFRA007|the government's agenda}}.
poiFRA001-desc: Franco-Iberia’s territorial ambitions and strategic positioning make it the spiritual successor to the Old European Union, but its vision is bolder and its methods more direct. With its sweeping claims over the western and southern parts of the continent, the Union aspires to establish itself as the unchallenged leader of Europe. Yet, internal tensions persist. Even decades after its inception, leaders within Franco-Iberia’s sprawling bureaucracy grapple with conflicting ideologies—from those advocating pan-European integration to hardliners intent on consolidating regional power at the expense of its neighbors.
poiFRA002-desc: However, this economic hegemony does not go unchallenged. Emerging powers, emboldened by new technologies and alliances, are eager to undermine Franco-Iberia’s dominance. To the north, the North Sea Alliance—a coalition of Scandinavian nations—wields its growing influence over polar trade routes, siphoning off lucrative markets once reliant on Mediterranean access. To the east, the INTEGR consolidates its economic and military might, posing an existential threat to Franco-Iberia’s ambitions. Even the Maghreb, long seen as a subordinate trading partner, is rising in prominence, driven by advancements in renewable energy and agricultural innovation, challenging Franco-Iberia’s control over southern trade corridors.
poiFRA003-desc:
Nobody in Franco-Iberia chose the phrase. It appeared on its own, first in the harbour taverns of Marseille and New Barcelona, and then everywhere: the Romans are back. A dockworker says it when a new customs tower rises over a Mediterranean port. A Padanian merchant mutters it over his ledgers when a Union tariff changes. In Athens it is said with a shrug, in Casablanca with a smirk, and in Berlin with a sneer.

It began as a joke and stopped being one. The comparisons are too easy to resist: a Senate that votes on everything, fortified ports, maglev lines laid where the old roads ran, a Mediterranean treated as a private lake, and an open conviction that the educated West has a duty to carry high culture to everyone else. Franco-Iberia has never claimed the title of empire, and nobody who uses the phrase believes it.

Over time it also became a name for the place itself. People speak of living under the Romans or beyond the Romans, the way their ancestors once spoke of the frontier of an older empire. A shipping route that crosses Union waters is the Roman leg. A town that has quietly adopted Union currency and Union schoolbooks has gone Roman. Franco-Iberians have taken the phrase back as well: Élodie’s admirers say it as a toast, and {{poiFRA008|Al-Hakim}}’s followers say it as an accusation.

As the year 2200 unfolds, the question is no longer whether the phrase is fair but how the story ends. Rome took centuries to build and longer to fall, and the people who say it most cheerfully are seldom the ones who have read the last chapter. Franco-Iberia’s ability to adapt, innovate and persevere may yet keep it a formidable force on the global stage. But the legions of history had their own bureaucrats squabbling over the frontier, too.
poiFRA004-desc:
Long wealthy, Élodie's lineage traces back to the nobility and privileged elite of Old France, extending a millennium before the Great Mistake. Her family's prestige and influence stemmed not from peerage but from the vast fortune amassed over the prior two centuries through holdings in agriculture, food processing, pharmaceuticals, and textiles.

Élodie entered the world at Europe's foremost fertility and maternity clinic in Braga as the only child of her parents. Raised in opulence along the Côte d'Azur and Costa del Sol, she became a media darling during her teenage years, though not always in a favorable light. Critics labeled her an isolationist and a European elitist, a reputation bolstered by her famously sharp tongue and incisive wit.

A staunch advocate of Western cultural traditions, Élodie believed it was the duty of the educated European elite to guide the masses, ensuring the preservation of high culture. She viewed the independence and sustainability of the new Union as the best means to achieve this vision.
poiFRA005-desc:
Franco-Iberia is undergoing a profound cultural renaissance, a revival reminiscent of the Renaissance and Enlightenment eras it holds dear. This resurgence is not merely about preserving the great artistic achievements of the past but fostering a dynamic environment for new generations of creators to explore and innovate. Through the Programe Artistice National, the Union has launched ambitious initiatives to nurture emerging artists and authors, encouraging them to build on its rich traditions while exploring new horizons in art and thought.

From the quietest rural villages to the busiest urban centers, citizens are drawn to {{poiFRA013|newly opened museums}}, theaters, and cinemas, celebrating both heritage and contemporary creativity. European works, enriched by cultural infusions from North Africa, have become a source of unifying pride. The Union's Directorate-General for Education and Culture actively promotes and exports this vibrant culture, spreading its influence across the globe through media and other channels.

In this flourishing environment, the Union's guiding ethos—trésors de l'esprit—remains clear: a person's true wealth lies in the knowledge and culture they carry and share, not in material accumulation. It is little wonder that, amid uncertainty and upheaval, many seek to join Franco-Iberia, drawn by its stability and dedication to the arts.
poiFRA006-desc: The Mediterranean Sea, transformed by climate change but still vital, is the lifeblood of Franco-Iberia’s economy. Now a vast inland ocean with expanded shorelines, it serves as a crucial artery for trade and commerce. The nation’s ports, fortified and modernized, are hubs of activity, channeling goods and resources to and from key trading partners such as the industrial powerhouse of Padania to the northeast, the revitalized city-states of Greece, and the resource-rich but politically fragmented Maghreb to the south. Franco-Iberia’s dominance over Mediterranean trade routes is a cornerstone of its wealth and influence, allowing it to maintain a level of prosperity that few other nations can rival in this new world order.
poiFRA007-desc: Franco-Iberia is governed by the Union Senate, a cornerstone of its democratic system, which deliberates and votes on all national matters. Esteemed worldwide as a model of effective democracy, the Senate fosters stability and a deep sense of civic engagement among its citizens. Direct votes from the populace are seamlessly processed through advanced computing systems, enabling efficient and transparent elections that strengthen public trust in the Union's governance.
poiFRA008-desc:
Al-Hakim is one of the most influential figures in the French political landscape. Born to an Algerian immigrant family in the now-flooded suburb of Saint-Ouen, North Paris, he grew up in the high-crime neighborhoods of the city. As a young man, he became involved in the criminal underworld. However, government initiatives aimed at reforming at-risk youth recognized Al-Hakim's potential and offered him opportunities to change his path.

Determined to rebuild his life, Al-Hakim immersed himself in economics, philosophy, and history. By the age of 23, he had written his first book, marking the beginning of a widely popular literary career. His success culminated in the release of the controversial yet best-selling Hakim Manifesto. The book, known for its sharp critique of 21st-century culture and lifestyles, blamed societal decline on a group he labeled the seres faux, while advocating for the empowerment of the seres vrais. Although historians dismissed the book as lacking scholarly rigor, its message resonated deeply with the people of Franco-Iberia.

Buoyed by widespread public support, Al-Hakim used his newfound wealth to establish the Partido Populaire, which quickly became the second most powerful political force in Franco-Iberia. His movement continues to attract a growing base of followers, driven by his promises of reform and social justice.

Ultimately, Al-Hakim envisions a future of complete social equality and comprehensive political restructuring, striving to ensure that the seres faux never regain influence over society.
poiFRA009-desc:
During the Dark Days, the north of old Italy slowly drifted away from {{poiFRA010|the rest of the country}}, economically and socially. Wealth gaps grew, and more and more northerners came to see themselves as a people apart. The flooding of the Po Valley made the boundary physical. Mounting tensions led to an independence referendum, and Padania became a sovereign state.

Thousands of rich investors and entrepreneurs followed from every corner of the globe. Padania is a second Switzerland: a haven for conglomerates and banks, a headquarters for chief executives, and a refuge where the rich of the world can indulge in luxury and keep their fortunes safe. Some look at it with disguised envy, others with open hatred, but nobody doubts its prosperity, or its value to Franco-Iberia as a trading partner.

Its face is Matteo Bossi, born in Padania before Padania existed. Never seen without a sharp suit and a spark in his eye, he is described by friends and enemies alike as innovative and honest. He inherited a modest contracting firm from his father, a fervent Padanian nationalist, and within ten years it was the first name on most industrial projects in Europe. In 2183 he folded his assets to run for mayor of Novara, a symbol of Padanian success in spite of the "corrupt Italians" and the "overbearing Franco-Iberians". Now he turns his eyes inward. Padania is free, but Bossi wants it to be a paradise, and truly independent of everyone, Paris included.
poiFRA010-desc:
When Padania voted to leave, many of old Italy's rich and powerful left with it and took their wealth north. What remained, Italia, was left with scraps, still reeling from the environmental refugee crisis, and its economy collapsed as investment stopped flowing. It can barely be called an economic power today.

The poor and desperate turned to the Partito Sociale, which rescued many from constant suffering with new social policies and a crackdown on exploitation. With the peninsula united under the Red Star, the Party puts the blame squarely on the capitalists of the north, the traitors who abandoned their nation for money.

Its rising figure is Ottaviano Acquati. His family fled the Po Valley cities that now lie underwater when old Italy ordered the evacuations, and he grew up poor, often leaving school to support them. His saving grace was a gift for law, learned from university textbooks in his spare time, and he became a formidable advocate. He joined the Partito Sociale to end the cycle of poverty he grew up in. As he sees it, Italia has two enemies: Padania, and Franco-Iberia, the self-styled liberator of Europe that shows nothing but contempt for the weakened nation-states and means to keep old Italy split in two. Italia sits in {{poiFRA012|the Mediterranean Bloc}} beside both of them, because it cannot afford to sit anywhere else, and Acquati means to change the terms from the inside.
poiFRA011-desc:
Greece is home to one of the oldest civilizations in Europe, and its people are proud owners of a history that spans millennia. The ruins of long-dead rulers overshadow its network nodes and high-tech construction yards, and its schools teach ancient history alongside augmentation. Whatever small tourism industry still exists in Europe, Greece has all but monopolized it.

Its mountains spared it the worst of the floods, of both water and refugees, and left it in a position of relative strength. Its revitalized city-states are among Franco-Iberia's most important partners in the Mediterranean.
poiFRA012-desc:
Franco-Iberia does not trade alone. Around it stands the Mediterranean Bloc: Franco-Iberia itself, {{poiFRA010|Italia}}, {{poiFRA009|Padania}}, {{poiFRA011|Greece}} and the Union of Maghreb, five economies bound together by the inland sea they share and by a common need to keep it open.

Apart from the gas fields of the Maghreb, the Bloc is poor in the fuels the old world ran on. It must buy most of its oil, and it pays for it with what it makes and what it moves: the iron, copper, bauxite and tungsten of its hills, the manufactures of Padania and Franco-Iberia, the harbours of Greece, and the phosphate, fields and sun of the Maghreb. Its strength is its ports, and its fear is losing them.

Its members do not love one another. Italia has not forgiven Padania for leaving, or Franco-Iberia for blessing it. Padania wants its independence respected by everyone, Paris included. The Maghreb is rising fast enough that some in the Union Senate have stopped calling it a junior partner. But to the north the North Sea Alliance is drawing trade away from the Mediterranean, and to the east INTEGR is drawing ever closer, and for now that is enough to keep the Bloc together.
poiFRA013-desc:
LysCore—Lys, Science, Culture et Ouverture—is Franco-Iberia’s independent cultural and historical corporation, built to make humanity’s memory impossible to erase. Publicly chartered and funded through a combination of state investment and private partnerships, it operates at arm’s length from the government: accountable to the public, but free to decide what it preserves, how it investigates, and where its work takes it.

Its mandate is vast: to seek out, recover and safeguard the records of human civilization wherever they remain—in public collections, private hands, threatened archives, abandoned settlements or the digital debris of a vanished world. Documents, artworks, scientific findings, oral histories and everyday objects all belong in its care. Each acquisition is authenticated, catalogued and preserved, then added to a secure, continually expanding archive accessible across borders.

LysCore was founded on a conviction born from catastrophe: history cannot warn us if its evidence is lost, hidden or forgotten. Preservation, in its view, is not enough. Knowledge must circulate. Through open archives, traveling exhibitions, public campaigns, research fellowships and international cultural summits, LysCore brings the past into active conversation with the present—and puts its findings within reach of citizens, scholars and decision-makers alike.

To its supporters, LysCore is a shared vault for the memory of humankind. To its critics, it is an institution with an extraordinary power to shape what the world remembers. It accepts the burden that comes with that power: to preserve without claiming ownership, to inform without dictating conclusions, and to keep humanity’s record alive—even when the truth it contains is uncomfortable.
